scenes.heading: Broadcast Join
scenes.narration: Let's take a deep look at Broadcast Join and how it works under the hood in Spark.

scenes.heading: What a broadcast join is
items: Ships a small table to every executor
scenes.narration: A broadcast join is Spark's strategy for joining a large table with a small one efficiently. Instead of shuffling both sides across the network, Spark sends a full copy of the small table to every executor. Each executor then joins its local partitions of the big table against that in-memory copy, avoiding the expensive shuffle entirely.

scenes.heading: Broadcast vs sort-merge join

left.title: Broadcast hash join
points: Small side must fit in memory

scenes.narration: A broadcast hash join wins when one side is small enough to fit in memory, because it eliminates shuffling the large table. A sort-merge join is the fallback when both sides are large: it shuffles and sorts both tables by the join key before merging them. The broadcast path is dramatically cheaper, but only when the small side truly fits.

scenes.code:
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast

big = spark.read.parquet("/data/transactions")   # billions of rows
dims = spark.read.parquet("/data/countries")     # a few hundred rows

joined = big.join(broadcast(dims), "country_id")
joined.explain()  # BroadcastHashJoin in the plan
scenes.heading: Forcing a broadcast
scenes.narration: The broadcast hint wraps the small countries table so Spark ships it to every executor. The transactions table stays put and is joined locally, so no shuffle of the billions of rows occurs. The explain output should show a BroadcastHashJoin, confirming the strategy. Spark can also choose this automatically when a side is under the autoBroadcastJoinThreshold.

Spark broadcasts automatically when it estimates the small side is below the threshold, which defaults to ten megabytes. Broadcasting a table that is too large can trigger driver or executor out-of-memory errors, so size the small side and the threshold carefully.
